results.reason: Issue 1 cites §2.2's automatic five-year renewal and the 270/240-day notice window. It computes the window as October 3 to November 2, 2026 against the June 30, 2027 expiry. It explains the five-year lock-in and the MAPC step-up, and recommends a tolling amendment or a protective notice before the window closes.

Issue 2 cites §5.3's 30-day window, the August 21 receipt and the roughly September 20, 2026 deadline. It notes the 'deemed to have accepted' consequence and says the client must confirm whether an objection was sent. It also recommends seeking commercial relief through negotiation.

Issue 5 says §11.1 covers any distribution-related claim, including product-defect claims, and is uncapped under §12.3(a). It notes §11.2 is subject to the cap and calls the arrangement lopsided. It recommends narrowing §11.1 to Halvorsen's own fault and carving §11.2 out of the cap.

Issue 4 says Amendment §3.1 replaces §12.3 and deletes the §9 recall carve-out. It explains that recall reimbursement is now subject to the 12-month cap, which a large recall could exceed, and recommends restoring §12.3(b).

Issue 3 identifies Delaware law and Wilmington exclusive jurisdiction under Amendment §6 and the conflict with New York law and the New York County forum in §17. It says the amendment likely prevails under §1.4 and recommends restoring §17.
The response states the Notice was delivered August 21, 2026.
The response states the Initial Term ends June 30, 2027.
Issue 3 states that under §1.4 'written amendments' rank first, so Delaware likely wins.
The response is a memorandum to the Partner. Each issue gives Where, Why it matters and Recommended fix, except the brief cleanup list in Issue 14, which still names sections and suggests fixes.
The response concludes that recall reimbursement is now capped, not that it remains outside the cap.
The response expressly recognizes the Delaware provisions in the First Amendment.
